items: Topic 03 got a signal to the end of a nerve. This topic is about the gap — and how the message jumps it.
Almost every synapse solves the gap chemically: electricity becomes a squirt of transmitter, which becomes electricity again on the other side.
That looks wasteful, and it is — but it buys three things a plain wire could never give: one-way traffic, the option to inhibit, and the ability to adjust the strength of the connection.
This is also where medicine lives: nerve gases, muscle relaxants, botox, myasthenia gravis and most psychiatric drugs all act in this gap.
A synapse is the junction where one excitable cell passes a message to the next.
Two kinds exist: chemical (the vast majority — a transmitter crosses a gap) and electrical (rare — current flows directly through gap junctions).
Chemical is slower but flexible; electrical is instantaneous but rigid.

blocks.x: A neuron by itself is useless — it only matters because it can talk to the next cell. This topic is about that conversation: the physical junction where one cell hands a message to another, and everything that can go right or wrong in that handoff.
▶️Cell to Cell CommunicationVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Cell-to-cell communication (overview)
blocks.def: The means by which impulses are transmitted from one cell to another — a key facet of every biological system. Communication happens via the liberation of signal molecules like hormones and neurotransmitters, which initiate their action by binding to receptors and generating a response. Communication may occur nerve cell to nerve cell, nerve cell to muscle, or nerve cell to gland.

blocks.name: Synapse
blocks.def: The site of transmission of information between cells. A typical synapse consists of a presynaptic cell and a postsynaptic cell.

blocks.name: Two categories of synapse
blocks.def: Electrical synapses (found at gap junctions) and chemical synapses (found at synaptic clefts) — fundamentally different mechanisms of handing off the signal.

items: The sequence, every time: action potential arrives → calcium enters the terminal → vesicles fuse and release transmitter → transmitter crosses the cleft → it binds receptors → the next cell's voltage changes.
Calcium is the trigger. Electrical signal in, chemical signal out — calcium is the translator between them.
The result is not automatically a new impulse. It is either an EPSP (makes firing more likely) or an IPSP (makes firing less likely).
Action potentials are not generated at the synapse itself, because the dendrites and cell body have too few voltage-gated sodium channels. The decision is made further along, at the axon hillock.
The signal must be cleared afterwards — by enzymes, reuptake, or diffusion — or the message would never end.
Think of it as passing a note across a gap rather than shouting: slower, but the note can say 'stop' as easily as 'go'.
Most antidepressants work by blocking reuptake, leaving the transmitter in the cleft longer — a direct manipulation of the last step above.

blocks.cap: A chemical synapse: vesicles, the synaptic cleft, and postsynaptic receptors.

blocks.name: Synapse between neurons (definition)
blocks.def: The junction between two neurons. Transmission here is mostly CHEMICAL. The presynaptic membrane may be the terminal of an axon; the postsynaptic membrane may be a dendrite, soma, or axon.

blocks.name: Synaptic cleft
blocks.def: The physical space between the presynaptic and postsynaptic cells, about 20 nanometers wide. Critically, an <term d="A brief, all-or-nothing electrical signal that sweeps along a nerve or muscle cell.">action potential</term> CANNOT cross this cleft directly — the electrical signal must be converted into a chemical one to make the jump.

blocks.name: How the signal actually crosses the cleft
blocks.def: The nerve impulse is carried across by chemicals called neurotransmitters, stored in synaptic vesicles at the end of the presynaptic neuron. The postsynaptic neuron has specific receptors for these neurotransmitters. This whole arrangement allows transmission in only ONE direction — from pre- to postsynaptic — never backward.

blocks.name: Sequence of events at a chemical synapse
blocks.def: An action potential at the presynaptic neuron opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels concentrated in the nerve terminal. Ca2+ flows into the cell. This Ca2+ causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the cell membrane, releasing <term d="A chemical messenger released by a nerve cell to pass a signal across a synapse.">neurotransmitter</term> by exocytosis. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. The transmitter-receptor complex causes a transient change in the postsynaptic membrane's conductance to one or more ions, producing a transient change in <term d="The difference in electrical charge between the inside and outside of a cell membrane.">membrane potential</term>.

blocks.name: EPSP (Excitatory Postsynaptic Potential)
blocks.def: A transient <term d="A shift of the membrane potential toward zero — the inside of the cell becomes less negative.">DEPOLARIZATION</term> of the postsynaptic membrane, caused by binding of an excitatory neurotransmitter — it makes it MORE likely the postsynaptic neuron will fire an action potential. Produced by an increase in BOTH Na+ and K+ conductance, but Na+ conductance dominates because Na+'s electrochemical gradient is steeper than K+'s. A single presynaptic input typically causes about a 1-2 mV depolarization. EPSPs can also be produced by agents that CLOSE K+ channels.

blocks.name: IPSP (Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential)
blocks.def: A transient <term d="When the inside of the cell becomes even more negative than its normal resting value.">HYPERPOLARIZATION</term> of the postsynaptic membrane, caused by binding of an inhibitory neurotransmitter — it makes it MORE DIFFICULT for the postsynaptic neuron to fire. Produced by an increase in K+ efflux, an increase in Cl- influx, closure of Na+ channels, or closure of Ca2+ channels — several different mechanisms can all produce the same hyperpolarizing effect.

blocks.name: Why action potentials aren't produced right at the synapse
blocks.def: The postsynaptic potential change (EPSP or IPSP) is itself only a <term d="A small local change in membrane charge whose size depends on how strong the stimulus was.">graded potential</term> — it must summate with other inputs elsewhere on the cell before <term d="The minimum strength of stimulus needed to trigger an action potential.">threshold</term> is reached and an actual action potential is generated (typically at the axon hillock).

blocks.name: How neurotransmitter action is terminated
blocks.def: Neurotransmitter action ends through breakdown by a specific enzyme in the synaptic cleft, or through transmitter uptake — reabsorption of the breakdown products by the presynaptic neuron via endocytosis, which are then used (with energy from mitochondria) to resynthesize more neurotransmitter. This termination step is essential — without it, the synapse would remain permanently switched on.

items: Cells are physically joined by gap junctions, so current flows straight through — no transmitter, no delay.
Advantages: essentially instantaneous, and usually bidirectional.
Limitations: they can generally only excite, not inhibit, and they cannot be finely tuned.
Used where speed and synchrony beat subtlety — which is exactly why cardiac muscle uses them.
This is the same wiring you met in the heart: gap junctions let a whole chamber contract as one.

blocks.x: ▶️Chemical vs Electrical SynapseVideo · Science with Tal

blocks.name: Electrical synapses
blocks.def: Rare, and FASTER than chemical synapses. Occur at gap junctions, where the pre- and postsynaptic membranes are only about 2-3 nm apart, allowing ions to pass directly from one neuron's cytoplasm into the next. An action potential passes from presynaptic to postsynaptic neuron almost INSTANTANEOUSLY.

blocks.name: Key differences of electrical vs chemical synapses
blocks.def: Electrical synapses often lack the directional specificity of chemical synapses — they may transmit a signal in EITHER direction, unlike the strictly one-way chemical synapse. They also do NOT integrate signals the way chemical synapses do (there's no summation or modulation possible, the signal just passes through directly).

sections.title: Synaptic Integration — Adding Up Thousands of Inputs

items: A single neuron may receive thousands of inputs at once, some saying go, others saying stop.
It adds them all up and fires only if the total reaches threshold — a continuous vote, not a single command.
Temporal summation: the same input fires repeatedly in quick succession, so the effects stack before they fade.
Spatial summation: different inputs fire at the same moment in different places, and their effects add together.
This is where the nervous system does its actual computing — not in any one synapse, but in the arithmetic of many.
Temporal = one person knocking repeatedly until you answer. Spatial = several people knocking at once. Either way, you get up.
It is why a single mosquito bite is ignorable but many at once become unbearable.

blocks.x: A single neuron might have thousands of synapses landing on its dendrites and cell body — thousands of separate 'votes,' some saying yes (excite), some saying no (inhibit). The neuron has to somehow add all these votes up and decide, with just one output (its axon), whether to fire or not.

blocks.name: Synaptic integration (overview)
blocks.def: One neuron can have thousands of synapses on its body and dendrites — many inputs, but only ONE output. The output through the axon is called the Grand Postsynaptic Potential (GPSP), which is the SUM of all excitatory and inhibitory potentials from all of that cell's synapses.

blocks.name: Facilitation vs inhibition (in synaptic integration)
blocks.def: If there are MORE excitatory potentials than inhibitory ones, the result is facilitation (increased likelihood of firing). If there are MORE inhibitory potentials than excitatory ones, the result is inhibition of the impulse (decreased likelihood of firing).

blocks.name: Two types of summation
blocks.def: Spatial and temporal — both allow for 'grading' of the nervous response, letting the neuron respond proportionally rather than in an all-or-nothing way at the input stage.

blocks.name: Temporal summation
blocks.def: A single action potential in a presynaptic neuron produces a 1-mV EPSP. If two action potentials fire in QUICK SUCCESSION from the SAME presynaptic neuron, two EPSPs are produced, and the second summates on the falling edge (tail) of the first — because the membrane temporarily stores the charge of the first EPSP, the charge from the second adds to it, producing a potential twice as large as either alone. This depends heavily on the DURATION of the synaptic potential and the membrane's 'time constant.'

blocks.name: Spatial summation
blocks.def: Occurs when MORE THAN ONE presynaptic neuron stimulates a postsynaptic neuron SIMULTANEOUSLY. Action potentials produced at the same time in different presynaptic neurons elicit EPSPs that summate to produce a combined EPSP larger than any individual one. This depends on the membrane's 'space constant' — how far a local potential can spread before dying out.

sections.title: Presynaptic Inhibition — Turning Down the Volume Before It Even Plays

items: Ordinary inhibition acts on the receiving cell. Presynaptic inhibition acts on the sending terminal — reducing how much transmitter is released in the first place.
Mechanism: it limits calcium entry into the terminal, so fewer vesicles are released.
GABA does this through GABA-A (chloride channels) and GABA-B (which reduces calcium entry and increases potassium exit).
The advantage is precision: it can silence one specific input without dampening the whole neuron.
It is turning down one instrument in the mix, rather than turning down the whole speaker.
Benzodiazepines and alcohol both boost GABA activity — which is why they calm, sedate and impair coordination.

blocks.name: Presynaptic inhibition
blocks.def: An axoaxonal inhibition of a stimulatory presynaptic neuron, occurring BEFORE it even reaches its synapse. Serves as a means of adjusting synaptic strength and/or preventing excessive transmitter release.

blocks.name: Sequence of events in presynaptic inhibition
blocks.def: A THIRD neuron influences the activity between a stimulatory presynaptic ending and a postsynaptic neuron. An action potential in this third neuron releases a transmitter that INHIBITS voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on the original presynaptic terminal — this decreases presynaptic Ca2+ influx during that terminal's own action potential, which reduces the amount of transmitter it releases downstream.

blocks.name: GABA-A and GABA-B mechanisms in presynaptic inhibition
blocks.def: In addition to inhibiting voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, some transmitters ALSO activate Cl- conductance (e.g., via GABA-A receptors, producing fast IPSPs) or activate voltage-gated K+ channels (e.g., via GABA-B receptors, producing slower, longer-lasting IPSPs) — two different GABA <term d="A protein that recognises and binds a specific signal molecule, triggering a response in the cell.">receptor</term> subtypes, two different speeds of inhibition.

items: A transmitter is not intrinsically excitatory or inhibitory — the receptor decides the effect. The same molecule can excite one target and inhibit another.
Neuroexciters (e.g. glutamate, acetylcholine at many sites) push the postsynaptic cell toward threshold.
Neuroinhibitors (e.g. GABA, glycine) push it away from threshold.
Balance matters more than either alone: too much excitation causes seizures; too much inhibition causes coma.
Acetylcholine is the classic proof: it speeds up nothing but slows the heart via muscarinic receptors, while contracting skeletal muscle via nicotinic ones. Same molecule, opposite outcomes.

blocks.name: Neurotransmitters (general)
blocks.def: Endogenous chemicals that transmit signals from a neuron to a target cell across a synapse. Broadly divided into neuroexciters and neuroinhibitors.

blocks.name: Neuroexciters
blocks.def: Cause DEPOLARIZATION of the postsynaptic membrane, resulting in EPSPs. Examples: acetylcholine (ACh, at skeletal muscle), norepinephrine (NE), epinephrine (E), dopamine (DA), aspartate, and glutamate.

blocks.name: Neuroinhibitors
blocks.def: Cause HYPERPOLARIZATION of the postsynaptic membrane, resulting in IPSPs. Examples: GABA, glycine, and (notably) ACh itself — but acting on HEART muscle rather than skeletal muscle. This is a great reminder that the SAME neurotransmitter can be excitatory or inhibitory depending entirely on which receptor and tissue it's acting on.

sections.title: The Neuromuscular Junction — Where Nerve Meets Muscle

items: The NMJ is a chemical synapse specialised for absolute reliability — unlike neuron-to-neuron synapses, it is designed so that every nerve impulse produces a muscle impulse.
Reliability is built in physically: junctional folds pack in huge numbers of receptors, and far more ACh is released than the minimum needed (a 'safety factor').
The sequence: impulse arrives → calcium enters → ACh released → ACh binds nicotinic receptors → end-plate potential (EPP) → muscle action potential → contraction.
Acetylcholinesterase then destroys ACh within milliseconds, so one nerve impulse causes exactly one twitch.
Quantal release: ACh leaves in fixed packets (vesicles). A single spontaneous packet gives a tiny MEPP; hundreds together give a full EPP that crosses threshold.
MEPPs are the synapse 'idling' — small leaks happening constantly, even when the nerve is silent.
The safety factor is why healthy muscle never randomly fails to respond — and why disease has to destroy a lot of receptors before weakness appears.

blocks.cap: The neuromuscular junction: ACh vesicles, the cleft, and the motor end plate’s junctional folds.

blocks.name: Neuromuscular (myoneural) junction
blocks.def: The synapse of a motor neuron's terminal with the motor end plate of a muscle fiber. At the junction, the motor nerve loses its myelin sheath and branches into several terminal buttons, each packed with thousands of vesicles filled with acetylcholine (ACh) and mitochondria.

blocks.name: Synaptic troughs and junctional folds
blocks.def: The terminal buttons sit implanted in small invaginations of the <term d="The cell membrane of a muscle fibre.">sarcolemma</term> called synaptic troughs, which are themselves thrown into folds called junctional folds — this folding dramatically increases the surface area available for ACh receptors.

blocks.name: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)
blocks.def: A fast-acting enzyme, confined to the synaptic cleft and bound to the postjunctional membrane and other membranes, that DEGRADES acetylcholine — this is the enzyme responsible for shutting the signal off after each impulse.

blocks.name: Neuromuscular transmission — the full sequence
blocks.def: A nerve action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and allowing Ca2+ influx. Ca2+ causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release ACh by exocytosis. ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end plate, opening receptor-coupled Na+ and K+ channels. This produces a transient depolarization called the end-plate potential (EPP).

blocks.name: End-plate potential (EPP)
blocks.def: A local response that acts as a current sink, electrotonically depolarizing the adjacent regions of the muscle cell. When depolarization of these adjacent regions reaches threshold, a true action potential is generated and conducted into the cell to initiate contraction.

blocks.name: Termination of neuromuscular transmission
blocks.def: ACh that dissociates from the nicotinic receptors is degraded into INACTIVE choline and acetate by AChE. Most of the resulting choline is returned to the presynaptic membrane by a Na+-choline cotransporter, where it recombines with acetyl-CoA to reform ACh, which is stored back in vesicles — a full recycling loop.

blocks.name: Quantal release of ACh
blocks.def: ACh is released in discrete packets called quanta — the amount of ACh contained in a single vesicle is 'a quantum' of ACh.

blocks.name: Miniature End Plate Potential (MEPP)
blocks.def: Results from SPONTANEOUS quantal release of ACh (i.e., without any nerve impulse triggering it) — leads to small transient depolarizations of about 0.5 mV, occurring at a frequency of roughly 1 per second. Background 'noise' at the junction, essentially.

blocks.name: End Plate Potential (EPP) vs MEPP
blocks.def: The true EPP results from a nerve impulse evoking a HUGE quantal release (about 300 quanta) of ACh at once, leading to depolarization of the postjunctional membrane sufficient to trigger <term d="The chain of events linking the electrical signal at the membrane to the actual mechanical contraction.">excitation-contraction coupling</term> and actual muscular activity — a real signal, not background noise.

sections.title: When the Neuromuscular Junction Goes Wrong

items: Every drug and toxin here attacks one specific step of the sequence above — learn the sequence and the pharmacology falls out of it.
Non-depolarizing blockers (curare-like) compete with ACh at the receptor → flaccid paralysis. Depolarizing blockers (suxamethonium) over-stimulate, causing brief twitching then paralysis.
Hemicholiniums block choline uptake (no raw material); vesamicol blocks packaging into vesicles.
Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release → paralysis. Black widow venom does the opposite — massive release → spasm.
AChE inhibitors stop breakdown, so ACh accumulates and the effect is amplified — the basis of both nerve agents and myasthenia treatment.
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune attack on nicotinic receptors: fewer receptors → the safety factor is lost → weakness that worsens with use and improves with rest.
Botox is botulinum toxin used deliberately — paralysing tiny facial muscles by blocking ACh release, exactly as described above.
Surgical anaesthesia uses these blockers routinely, which is why an anaesthetist must breathe for the patient: the diaphragm is skeletal muscle too.
Classic myasthenia story: a patient whose eyelids droop and speech slurs as the evening goes on, then recovers after sleep.

blocks.name: Neuromuscular blockers (NMBAs)
blocks.def: Substances that interfere with neural transmission between motor neurons and skeletal muscle, causing skeletal muscle PARALYSIS. Their site of action may be junctional, postjunctional, or prejunctional.

blocks.name: Non-depolarizing blockers
blocks.def: Example: tubocurarine. These are ACh receptor ANTAGONISTS, competitively inhibiting ACh at nicotinic receptors of the neuromuscular membrane. At higher doses they cause physical blockade of the receptors, preventing depolarization of the motor end plate. Their effect can be REVERSED by cholinesterase inhibitors (which raise ACh levels enough to out-compete the blocker).

blocks.name: Depolarizing blockers
blocks.def: Example: succinylcholine (structurally, two ACh molecules joined together). These are ACh receptor AGONISTS — they cause slow, prolonged depolarization of the motor end plate. Prolonged depolarization causes all receptors to remain inactive, so no further action potentials can be conducted. Unlike ACh itself, these agents are resistant to degradation by acetylcholinesterase and are instead degraded by butyrylcholinesterase, a <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">plasma</term> cholinesterase.

blocks.name: Prejunctional blockers
blocks.def: Drugs/chemicals that impair ACh formation, storage, or release — acting before the signal even reaches the synapse.

blocks.name: Hemicholiniums
blocks.def: Block the Na+-choline transporter, inhibiting choline uptake into the presynaptic terminal. Prolonged treatment depletes choline and therefore ACh synthesis, since choline uptake is the rate-limiting step in making new ACh.

blocks.name: Botulinum toxin
blocks.def: Blocks the RELEASE of ACh by preventing vesicular docking at the presynaptic membrane — the vesicles are full of ACh but can never fuse and release it.

blocks.name: Black widow spider venom
blocks.def: Disrupts synaptic vesicles and depletes the nerve endings of ACh — essentially the opposite mechanism to botulinum toxin (it causes uncontrolled dumping rather than blocking release), but with the same end result of ACh depletion.

blocks.name: Vesamicol
blocks.def: Blocks ACh transport INTO storage vesicles, thus limiting how much ACh is available to be released even if the release machinery itself works fine.

blocks.name: Junctional blockers (AChE inhibitors)
blocks.def: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase blocks neuromuscular transmission by causing ACh to ACCUMULATE at the junction, producing MAINTAINED (rather than transient) depolarization of the motor end plate. This leads to convulsions, then paralysis, and death — usually from paralysis of the diaphragm (breathing muscle). This is the mechanism of action of many insecticides and nerve gases containing organophosphates.

blocks.name: Myasthenia gravis
blocks.def: A chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disease causing varying degrees of skeletal muscle weakness. Caused by circulating antibodies (produced by the patient's own immune system) that block, alter, or destroy ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction, preventing the muscle from contracting properly. Though any voluntary muscle may be affected, the muscles controlling the eyes/eyelids, facial expression, and swallowing are most frequently involved. Treated with anticholinesterase agents (e.g., neostigmine, pyridostigmine), which allow ACh to accumulate in the synaptic cleft, improving transmission and muscle strength — and can also be treated by thymectomy (surgical removal of the thymus, which is often implicated in producing the autoantibodies).

sections.title: The Autonomic Neuroeffector Junction & Its Two Chemical Systems

items: The autonomic 'synapse' is much less tidy than the NMJ: there is no neat end-plate. Axons run over the tissue in a mesh, releasing transmitter from swellings called varicosities.
The result is a spray, not a handshake — transmitter diffuses over a wider area to many cells at once, which suits organs that must act as a whole.
Cholinergic fibres release ACh; adrenergic fibres release noradrenaline.
The receptor decides the outcome: muscarinic (G-protein-coupled, via second messengers) for ACh at effectors, and adrenergic α/β subtypes for noradrenaline.
Denervation hypersensitivity: cut the nerve supply and the target becomes more sensitive, because it makes extra receptors — a tissue turning up its hearing when nobody is speaking.
This is why one surge of adrenaline can affect your heart, lungs, gut and pupils simultaneously — the delivery system is designed to be broad, not targeted.
It is also the direct doorway into Topic 09: from here on, everything is about which transmitter meets which receptor.

blocks.name: Neuroeffector junction
blocks.def: The termination of a postganglionic autonomic nerve at any smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or secretory tissue — the autonomic nervous system's equivalent of the neuromuscular junction, but for involuntary targets.

blocks.name: Autonomic ground plexus and varicosities
blocks.def: Near the effector tissue, autonomic axons branch and intermingle to form the autonomic ground plexus. The axons partially lose their Schwann cell covering and terminate as a series of varicosities (swellings) close to the target organ, occurring at 5-10 micrometer intervals. Unlike the neuromuscular junction's tight, defined synapse, this arrangement means the transmitter is released more diffusely, affecting a broader area, acting more slowly, and lasting longer.

blocks.name: Cholinergic mechanism (fibers that release ACh)
blocks.def: Cholinergic fibers include: somatic motor fibers, ALL autonomic preganglionic fibers, ALL parasympathetic postganglionic fibers, and sympathetic postganglionic fibers innervating sweat glands and a few skeletal muscle blood vessels. Postganglionic ACh acts via muscarinic receptors, which are blocked by the drug atropine, and are characterized by a prolonged response (a few seconds) that can be either excitatory or inhibitory depending on the target organ.

blocks.name: Muscarinic receptor second-messenger mechanisms
blocks.def: Muscarinic receptors control ion channels via second messengers, by: stimulating Gi (which inhibits adenylate cyclase, decreasing cAMP), stimulating DAG and IP3 production, or increasing K+ conductance via a G protein — the same core second-messenger toolkit from <term d="The body's ability to keep its internal conditions steady despite changes going on outside.">Homeostasis</term>, applied here to autonomic signaling.

blocks.name: Adrenergic mechanism (fibers that release catecholamines)
blocks.def: Adrenergic fibers secrete norepinephrine, dopamine, and epinephrine. Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers are adrenergic. Transmitter release is presumed to be via a Ca2+-mediated exocytosis process, similar to other synapses. Released norepinephrine is either taken back up by the presynaptic ending and postsynaptic/peripheral cells, or enzymatically degraded.

blocks.name: Adrenergic receptors (adrenoceptors)
blocks.def: A class of G protein-coupled receptors that are targets of the catecholamines. Two main groups: alpha-adrenergic and beta-adrenergic receptors, each further split into subtypes (alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, beta-2). Norepinephrine has a HIGHER affinity for alpha receptors; epinephrine has a higher affinity for beta receptors — this affinity difference is a key reason the two related hormones can produce somewhat different physiological effects.

blocks.name: Denervation hypersensitivity
blocks.def: An INCREASED sensitivity to neurotransmitters or their agonists in an effector organ AFTER it has been denervated (lost its nerve supply). Develops 7-14 days after denervation. May be due to: proliferation of receptors on the denervated tissue, spread and diffuseness of receptors across the cell surface (rather than confined to the junction), disappearance of the enzymes that normally degrade the transmitter, loss of transmitter uptake mechanisms, and an increased number of gap junctions in the denervated tissue. In short: cut off the normal supply, and the target tissue compensates by becoming hyper-responsive to whatever transmitter does reach it.

items: Calcium is the translator: it turns the electrical signal into a chemical one at every terminal.
EPSP moves toward threshold; IPSP moves away.
Temporal = one input over time; spatial = several inputs at once.
The NMJ never fails; brain synapses often do — that is a designed difference, not an accident.
Nicotinic = fast ion channel; muscarinic = slower G protein.

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: The synapse does not decide. It only nudges. The decision to fire is taken at the axon hillock, after all inputs are summed.
A transmitter is not 'excitatory' or 'inhibitory' by itself — the receptor decides. ACh excites skeletal muscle and slows the heart.
Botulinum blocks release; AChE inhibitors prolong action. Opposite ends of the same sequence — do not mix them up.
Presynaptic inhibition reduces release; postsynaptic inhibition resists the response. Different sites, different logic.
← Excitable Tissues (Topic 03): the impulse arriving at the terminal is where that topic ended and this one begins.
← Skeletal & Cardiac Muscle (Topics 04–05): the NMJ is the handover that starts every voluntary contraction; gap-junction synapses are what let the heart beat as one.
← Homeostasis (Topic 02): receptors, second messengers and amplification reappear here as the machinery of every synapse.
→ Autonomic Nervous System (Topic 09): the neuroeffector junction is literally the last section of this topic and the first idea of the next.
The one-line summary: electricity → chemistry → electricity, in one direction, with the option to say stop — and nearly every drug you will ever prescribe interferes with one step of it.

lines: Autocrine acts on the cell itself, paracrine on neighbours, endocrine through the bloodstream, and neural down a wired connection.
Gap junctions couple adjacent cytoplasms directly; synapses send a chemical across a cleft to a specific target.
Ligand-gated ion channels act in milliseconds; G-protein and second-messenger routes are slower to start but amplified and longer-lasting.
Steroid and thyroid hormones cross the membrane to intracellular receptors and alter transcription; peptides and catecholamines work at the surface.
